title: Cogentrex — Azure Development Deployment and Safe Delivery
purpose: Understand how a protected revision becomes an evidence-backed Azure development deployment without overstating production readiness.
limitations: This is derivative learning material, not canonical implementation evidence.
The observed target is one Azure VM running hardened Docker Compose; it is not Kubernetes, Container Apps, multi-region, or a production SLO.
PostgreSQL and Redis are persistent self-managed containers, not managed Azure database or cache services.

concepts.label: Protected Development Branch
concepts.summary: The dev branch accepts changes through pull requests with required checks rather than direct pushes.

teaching.definition: A protected integration branch is a repository control that makes reviewable change history and required checks prerequisites for merge.
teaching.responsibility: Reject direct pushes, force pushes, deletions, and merges whose backend, frontend, or image checks have not succeeded.
controls: No reviewer is required while Luis works alone
teaching.failure_behavior: A failed or missing check prevents merge; a merge is still not called deployed until CD and external smoke succeed.
teaching.why_it_matters: The branch boundary turns development discipline into an enforceable repository rule rather than a convention that can be bypassed during urgency.

concepts.boundary: Branch protection proves repository workflow, not code correctness, deployment success, or production governance.
concepts.narration: Cogentrex begins deployment evidence before Azure. A feature branch enters a protected dev pull request, required checks run, and only a reviewed passing revision can become the merge SHA used downstream.
concepts.scenario: A developer attempts a direct push to dev to skip a slow test.
options: Reject the push and require a PR with checks
concepts.scenario_explanation: The protected branch keeps the evidence chain consistent even when bypassing it would be convenient.

concepts.label: Required CI Gates
concepts.summary: Backend, frontend, browser, security, migration, documentation, and image checks prove the candidate revision before merge.

teaching.definition: Required CI is a revision-scoped verification layer that executes deterministic quality and packaging contracts before deployment authority is granted.
teaching.responsibility: Run lint, format, security, documentation, backend, frontend, browser, build, and image smoke checks against the proposed revision.
controls: Checks bind to the PR revision
teaching.failure_behavior: A timeout is not a pass, a skipped required job blocks progression, and stale success from another SHA cannot authorize merge.
teaching.why_it_matters: Agent systems combine runtime, persistence, browser, provider, and operational contracts; one narrow test suite cannot establish that the deployable unit is coherent.

concepts.boundary: CI proves deterministic contracts and image startup; it does not prove live provider quality or public endpoint readiness.
concepts.narration: Required CI evaluates the exact pull-request revision across backend, frontend, browser, security, migrations, documentation, and the built backend image. Only the named green checks permit merge.
concepts.scenario: Frontend tests pass but the migration roundtrip fails.
options: Block merge until the migration contract passes
concepts.scenario_explanation: The candidate revision is only as deployable as its failing required boundary.

concepts.label: Immutable ACR Images
concepts.summary: Backend and frontend images are published to Azure Container Registry under the merge SHA.

teaching.definition: An immutable deployment image is a packaged application artifact addressed by a revision identity that does not move after publication.
teaching.responsibility: Build the architecture-correct backend and frontend images, smoke them, and publish exact SHA references for deployment and rollback.
controls: No mutable latest tag as deployment truth
teaching.failure_behavior: A build or image smoke failure prevents publication; deployment never substitutes a locally built or differently tagged image.
teaching.why_it_matters: Rollback and evidence become ambiguous when a tag can point to different bytes over time. SHA-addressed images connect Git history to the runtime artifact.

concepts.boundary: Image immutability does not prove vulnerability-free dependencies, provenance signing, or runtime health after rollout.
concepts.narration: After merge, GitHub builds and smokes backend and frontend images, then publishes them to ACR under the merge SHA. The VM pulls those exact references, and rollback can name an earlier accepted SHA.
concepts.scenario: The latest tag changed after an incident began.
options: Rollback to the recorded accepted SHA
concepts.scenario_explanation: The accepted SHA is the stable link between source, image, and deployment evidence.

concepts.label: GitHub OIDC and UAMI
concepts.summary: GitHub exchanges a federated identity for narrowly scoped Azure access without storing a client secret.

teaching.definition: Federated workload identity lets GitHub Actions present an OIDC assertion that Azure maps to a user-assigned managed identity under an exact subject contract.
teaching.responsibility: Authenticate the deployment job and authorize only the Azure operations assigned through RBAC to the deployment identity.
teaching.failure_behavior: A subject mismatch, missing federation, wrong subscription, or insufficient role fails login or deployment rather than falling back to hidden credentials.
teaching.why_it_matters: Long-lived CI secrets are difficult to rotate and easy to overexpose. Federation narrows both credential lifetime and the repository context allowed to request access.

concepts.boundary: OIDC authenticates the deployment workload; it does not make every Azure role least privilege or verify end-user identity.
concepts.narration: The deployment job requests a GitHub OIDC assertion. Azure accepts it only for the configured repository and development environment, maps it to a UAMI, and evaluates RBAC for each operation.
concepts.scenario: A workflow from another branch presents an unmatched OIDC subject.
concepts.scenario_explanation: The federated credential must bind the exact trusted subject rather than broadening access after mismatch.

concepts.label: Runtime Identity and Key Vault
concepts.summary: The VM runtime identity accesses Azure services and secret references without embedding credentials in images.

teaching.definition: Runtime managed identity separates application authentication from deployment authentication and lets Azure issue short-lived tokens to the running VM workload.
teaching.responsibility: Resolve protected runtime configuration and authenticate DeepSeek requests without placing provider keys or client secrets in source, images, or workflow logs.
teaching.failure_behavior: Token acquisition, Key Vault access, or role failure makes readiness or provider execution fail; the runtime does not invent dummy credentials.
teaching.why_it_matters: Deployment authority and application authority have different purposes. Separate managed identities reduce blast radius and make each permission path explainable.

concepts.boundary: Managed identity does not remove the need for RBAC review, Key Vault rotation, or application-level authorization.
concepts.narration: The VM obtains tokens from Azure Managed Identity. Key Vault and Azure AI Services evaluate that runtime principal, keeping provider credentials outside Git, images, and ordinary environment disclosure.
concepts.scenario: The VM can reach Azure AI Services but lacks the required data-plane role.
concepts.scenario_explanation: Connectivity is not authorization; the missing role must be corrected explicitly.

concepts.label: Hardened VM Compose
concepts.summary: One Azure VM preserves the verified seven-service Compose topology and operational contracts.

teaching.definition: The Azure development target runs the same bounded service decomposition as the local baseline while adding cloud ingress, identity, monitoring, and deployment automation.
teaching.responsibility: Run gateway, frontend, backend, PostgreSQL, Redis, OpenTelemetry Collector, and sandbox with health dependencies and hardened container settings.
teaching.failure_behavior: Compose update, migration, dependency, media, or sandbox failure aborts deployment and preserves diagnostic state for rollback.
teaching.why_it_matters: The chosen target minimizes architecture drift: the sandbox and service boundaries remain explainable instead of being replaced merely to claim a managed platform.

concepts.boundary: A single VM has a larger failure domain and does not provide autoscaling, multi-zone availability, or managed database operations.
concepts.narration: Azure deployment preserves the seven-service topology: Caddy reaches the internal gateway, the backend depends on PostgreSQL and Redis, telemetry flows through the Collector, and the sandbox remains separate.
concepts.scenario: A cloud platform option cannot preserve the required sandbox boundary without redesign.
options: Choose the VM target and document the trade-off
Run tools in the API process
concepts.scenario_explanation: Deployment architecture must preserve accepted safety boundaries or explicitly re-earn them.

concepts.label: Sandbox Boundary in Cloud
concepts.summary: The runner remains networkless, read-only, capability-dropped, and reachable only through a private Unix socket.

teaching.definition: The sandbox is a separate execution container whose kernel-visible resources and communication channels are reduced before agent-requested code is allowed to run.
receives: CPU, memory, process, and output limits
teaching.responsibility: Execute supported code without project mounts, Docker socket, outbound network, writable root filesystem, or Linux capabilities.
teaching.failure_behavior: Unavailable runner, malformed frame, timeout, resource excess, or peer disconnect terminates the process group and returns a bounded failure.
teaching.why_it_matters: A public cloud endpoint increases exposure. Preserving the tested execution boundary is more important than adopting a platform that silently moves code into the API process.

concepts.boundary: Container isolation is not VM-grade hostile multi-tenant certification and still shares the VM kernel.
concepts.narration: The Azure target does not weaken the local sandbox contract. The backend sends bounded frames over a private Unix socket to a networkless, read-only, capability-dropped runner with resource and cleanup controls.
concepts.scenario: A deployment accidentally gives the sandbox the default Docker network.
options: Accept it because the VM has an NSG
concepts.scenario_explanation: The sandbox must preserve its own boundary even when host networking is separately protected.

concepts.label: Caddy TLS and External Smoke
concepts.summary: Caddy terminates public TLS and external smoke decides whether the deployed revision is observable at the development hostname.

teaching.definition: External smoke is a post-rollout acceptance check executed from outside the VM against the same HTTPS hostname a user reaches.
teaching.responsibility: Obtain and serve the certificate, route traffic, and prove public liveness/readiness plus the learning surface after remote deployment completes.
teaching.failure_behavior: DNS, ACME, Caddy, readiness, or route failure keeps the workflow red; a successful Run Command alone cannot make it green.
teaching.why_it_matters: Internal containers can be healthy while the real hostname is unavailable. External smoke closes the gap between machine state and user-reachable service.

concepts.boundary: A few successful smoke requests are not a load test, availability history, WAF, or production SLO.
concepts.narration: Caddy serves dev.cogentrex.com with automated TLS. The workflow then probes health, readiness, and learning from outside the VM; only those checks convert a rollout into observed development deployment evidence.
concepts.scenario: Run Command exits successfully but the public readiness URL fails.
options: Fail the smoke gate and investigate ingress/readiness
concepts.scenario_explanation: Deployment acceptance includes the user-facing endpoint, not only remote command completion.

concepts.label: Hosted Telemetry
concepts.summary: The OpenTelemetry Collector exports bounded request and dependency telemetry to Application Insights.

teaching.definition: Hosted telemetry projects safe operational metadata from the running service into a durable external observability system for cross-request investigation.
teaching.responsibility: Export request and dependency signals to Azure Monitor while preserving the policy that raw prompts, credentials, and hidden reasoning are not default telemetry fields.
teaching.failure_behavior: Inactive export or unavailable Collector fails configured readiness; missing telemetry never rewrites the Run Ledger as successful evidence.
teaching.why_it_matters: Public development operation needs evidence beyond local logs. Hosted signals make dependency latency and request outcomes inspectable without turning observability into a data leak.

concepts.boundary: Observed request/dependency records do not establish alert quality, retention policy, sampling strategy, cost control, or an SLO.
concepts.narration: The backend emits OTLP to the Collector, which exports safe request and dependency data into Application Insights. Live records prove the path, while production alerting and retention remain deferred.
concepts.scenario: A trace attribute contains a raw user prompt by default.
options: Remove or redact content before export
concepts.scenario_explanation: Hosted observability must preserve the same privacy boundary as local logging.

concepts.label: Backup, Rollback, and Roll-Forward
concepts.summary: Deployment creates protected PostgreSQL backups and keeps earlier SHA images available for rollback and recovery rehearsal.

teaching.definition: Rollback is a controlled transition from a failed or rejected revision to a previously accepted immutable revision, with durable state protected before change.
teaching.responsibility: Back up state, deploy or restore a known revision, rerun readiness and smoke, and retain enough evidence to roll forward after the rehearsal.
controls: Health and external smoke after transition
teaching.failure_behavior: Backup failure blocks rollout; unsuccessful rollback remains a failure rather than being reported as restored service.
teaching.why_it_matters: An immutable image is only useful when operators can select it, protect state, perform the transition, and prove the resulting service rather than trusting a manifest.

concepts.boundary: The rehearsal does not prove zero downtime, point-in-time recovery, off-site retention, regional failover, or an organization-approved RTO/RPO.
concepts.narration: Before rollout, Cogentrex creates a protected PostgreSQL backup. Operators can select the recorded previous SHA, rerun all gates, and then roll forward to the current SHA. Both directions were exercised in development.
concepts.scenario: The deployment image fails after a database migration begins.
options: Pretend the old app is compatible
Use backup and exact-SHA rollback procedures, then verify
concepts.scenario_explanation: State and application compatibility must be handled explicitly and verified after transition.
